paragraphs.heading: Mass times velocity
paragraphs.text: Momentum measures motion by multiplying how much mass an object has by its velocity, which also has a direction. It is written p, so p = mv. The letter comes from the Latin pellere, meaning to push or drive. In SI units it is counted in kg⋅m/s, kilogram metres per second, a unit equal in dimension to the newton-second.

paragraphs.heading: It points somewhere
paragraphs.text: Momentum is a vector, a quantity with both a size and a direction. A 1 kg model airplane flying due north at 1 m/s carries 1 kg⋅m/s of momentum pointing north, measured against the ground. Because momentum carries a direction, it lets you predict which way objects will move, and how fast, after they collide.

paragraphs.heading: Force changes momentum
paragraphs.text: Newton's second law ties momentum to force: the net force on a body equals how fast its momentum changes. If a steady force F acts for a time Δt, the momentum changes by Δp = FΔt. When the mass stays the same, this becomes the familiar F = ma, net force equals mass times acceleration.

paragraphs.heading: A worked example
paragraphs.text: Take a 1 kg model airplane that starts at rest and reaches 6 m/s due north in 2 seconds. Its momentum has changed by 6 kg⋅m/s due north. Spread over those 2 seconds, that is a change of 3 (kg⋅m/s)/s, which is the same number as the 3 newtons of net force needed to push it.

paragraphs.heading: The total stays fixed
paragraphs.text: In a closed system, one that swaps no matter with its surroundings and feels no outside forces, the total momentum does not change. This is the law of conservation of momentum, and it follows from Newton's laws. When two particles interact, the forces between them are equal in size and opposite in direction. So whatever momentum one gains, the other loses, and their sum stays the same.

paragraphs.heading: Far beyond everyday objects
paragraphs.text: Momentum does depend on the frame of reference you measure it from, but in any inertial frame it is conserved. The law reflects a basic symmetry of space and time called translational symmetry. Modified versions of it still hold in special relativity, electrodynamics, quantum mechanics and general relativity. In quantum mechanics, momentum and position are linked by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.
